maintopic: EFFECTS OF STRIKE IN UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: EFFECTS OF STRIKE IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Would the Minister of Defence Production care to comment upon the possible effects of the strike in the United States steel industry upon our own defence effort here in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: EFFECTS OF STRIKE IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the effect upon Canada will depend entirely on the duration of the strike. Our stocks are reasonably adequate for the immediate future and if the strike is settled in the next two or three weeks the effect may not be serious. There will be some effect on individual situations where steel that is on order with United States mills cannot come forward.
One of the more serious effects may be in connection with the movement of iron ore. As hon. members know, all the iron ore mines in the United States have been closed down along with the steel plants. This is the season of maximum water movement for iron ore and there may be repercussions as to delivery
[Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North).!
of quantities required by our steel plants, although it may be possible to divert certain iron ore from Canadian mines to Canadian steel plants for the time being.
All I can say is that it would be most unwise at this time to plan new projects using steel, but we are hopeful that the situation will be clarified in time to avoid any serious effect on construction now in progress.

I am concerned with what we are doing to obtain it and with what we are not doing. In no sense can anything I say be termed provincialism because I think every member of the House of Commons is concerned over this industry. I do not think there is any industry which affects every segment of our society as does the tourist industry. Many of these people will not be coming to this country this fall because, though they come for the sport, they like to take visible proof of their success home with them. If they are forbidden to export game they will at least be discouraged, and I would think definite steps should be taken to deal with the situation now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
It is always a matter of regret to me that the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare are covered in a few hours some afternoon or evening. I have always felt that a committee should investigate something as important to the people of Canada as sickness and the causes of death. For that reason I have always advocated a committee. When I started to look into the statistics on the prevalence of disease and the causes of death, I came upon some rather startling information. For that reason it appeared to me that more than a few hours should be spent on these matters.
I believe the members of the house are and should be interested in such things as the prevalence of disease in the country, and especially mortality rates. To show the importance of this matter I am going to discuss something which really does not come under this department but which, nevertheless, is listed as a cause of death in Canada. I refer to the number of accidental deaths. This does not concern the minister; but nevertheless it is listed under the causes of death. I find that I have to use statistics for the year 1948, because those were the only figures available to me. I find that accidental deaths, suicides excepted, in the Dominion of Canada amounted to the rather startling figure of 7,958 in 1948. Going back to the years 1946 and 1947, I find that this figure has been steadily creeping up.
From this one figure it would be difficult *to estimate the number of deaths from motor accidents and industrial accidents or from other accidents such as drowning. Two things stand out. I think the number of motor accidents in Canada is becoming appalling. Possibly our attention has been drawn to that in the last month or so because of the casualties suffered by the members of this party. We -are glad there have been no fatal results, but at the same time the figure of 7,958 is something to which this committee should give attention.
During the last winter the number of people who were burned to death, especially little children, throughout the whole of


Canada was something that bothered us a great deal. Practically every morning when we read the newspapers we found that some family had been wiped out by fire, or little children had been burned. So far as motor accidents are concerned, I know that every department of highways, every minister of highways of every province in the dominion is doing his best, both by publicity and warning the people over the radio, to cut down the number of accidents. In spite of that we still have this ghastly toll of 7,958 deaths. I am quite sure the number of people killed in industrial accidents would be comparatively small in relation to the number killed in motor accidents. As our population increases, no doubt the number of these accidents will become greater. On Memorial day in the United States the casualty list went up to something like 400 or 450. When we are considering immigration, bringing people into this country, and thus building up our population, these seem to be such useless and unnecessary deaths. Accidents will happen; but a toll of 7,958 is something to which this committee could well give some consideration, even if it is outside the ordinary duties of the minister or this department to do something about these deaths. I therefore recommend to the committee that, allowing just a little bit of leeway, Mr. Chairman, we should have some discussion on measures to prevent this sort of thing in this country.
I now come to the principal causes of death in Canada. Though it is a rather morbid subject, we cannot fully analyse the work of the department and the position of health in Canada unless we give consideration to these figures, because these statistics are all-important in a consideration of health estimates.
At the top of the list, in the first ten main causes of death in Canada from all agencies, I find that deaths from diseases of the heart amounted to 33,901. I find that cancer is on the increase, although our population is increasing; and in the last year for which I have statistics 16,258 people died of cancer. The next largest cause of death was intracranial lesions. That, of course, might mean anything occurring, but I think it refers principally to people dying of strokes and cerebral accidents. Violent deaths were in fourth place, the matter I was considering before. Nephritis accounted for 6,805; diseases of infancy, 7,045; pneumonia, 5,700; tuberculosis-and I include in that figure tuberculosis of all kinds-4,773; disease of the arteries, 2,349; and influenza, 911. In consideration of the tenth category I gave, diseases of the arteries, possibly some of those could have been added ip with No. 3 on the

list, casualties from intracranial lesions, because many of those were owing to what we call cerebral accidents.
There are, however, some bright spots when we look over this table. Diphtheria has almost been wiped out as a cause of death. In the last year for which I have statistics 86 people died of diphtheria. Tuberculosis has been greatly reduced. With the campaign that is going on at the present time in the province of Ontario I think this figure for tuberculosis will be steadily reduced as the years go by. But as the age of the population increases the probability of death will be greater from diseases which mainly affect older people. For instance, cancer and heart disease may account for a larger proportion of the deaths than formerly. When the age to which people in Canada live is increased, it is normal to believe that in their later years some weakness will become apparent that will carry them off. According to the statistics,, an increasing number of heart cases and cancer are unfortunately making their appearance. In analysing these statistics we must bear in mind the fact that while heart disease and cancer are increasing, there may be a reason for these increasing numbers finding their way into our statistics.
As to heart disease, one is struck by the number of cases of coronary disease occurring at the present time, especially among younger people in the thirties and forties, not in the older group to which I have referred. From reading the press, we are all aware of the number of prominent businessmen or men who have taken an active part in the affairs of our country who are suddenly wiped out owing to coronary disease. I shall say something later about research with regard to this disease. It is becoming a problem; there is no doubt about that.
So far as older people are concerned, while cancer is increasing-and this would refer also to people in the younger age groups-one must remember that the population is increasing, and that possibly we are getting better methods of diagnosis than we formerly had. This fact would probably be one reason for the statistics showing an increase in the number of cases in our country.

speechtext: Our statistics are better. Our techniques are better.

Yes. The techniques used in building up those statistics are much better. Nevertheless, making allowance for an increasing population and for the fact that there is better diagnosis with regard to this disease of cancer, we have a problem in the fact that 16,258 deaths from cancer occurred during the last year for which we have statistics. Possibly one should also look at the
Supply-Health and Welfare number of cases where, because of early treatment, deaths from this disease were avoided. In mentioning this matter I should like to refer to the prevalence of the disease in this country. In doing that I shall also refer to the necessity for opportunity for early diagnosis and treatment not only to people living in urban centres but throughout the whole of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the dinner recess I was discussing mortality rates in Canada, and the incidence of certain diseases.
I wish now to discuss the matter of infantile mortality in Canada. I am glad to say the rate in Canada has been dropping steadily. Possibly there are good reasons for that, because increased hospitalization, as well as widespread pre-natal and post-natal care have cut down the percentages of deaths. But there are other factors involved, such as improved water supplies, improved sanitation and the pasteurization of milk, which have had a great deal to do with the cutting down of the mortality rate.
I am going to give the committee the mortality rates in other countries in the world, by way of a comparison with Canada. The first country on the list, and the one with the lowest mortality rate in the world, is Iceland. The figure I give for Iceland is the 1947 figure, whereas the others I shall give are those for 1948. Iceland had an infantile mortality rate of 22, New Zealand, 22; Sweden, 23; Australia, 28; The Netherlands, 29; Norway, 30; England and Wales, 34; the United States, 32; Denmark, 35; the Jewish portion of Israel, 35; Switzerland, 36; the white population in the Union of South Africa, 37. Then I come to Canada with a rate of 44, exclusive of the Northwest Territories.
It is interesting to compare this over-all rate of 44 with the provincial rates. In British Columbia it is 33; Prince Edward Island, 34; Ontario, 35; Alberta, 39; Nova Scotia, 39; Saskatchewan, 40; Manitoba, 41; Quebec, 54; New Brunswick, 61; and I give the rate for Newfoundland before joining the rest of Canada as standing at 74.
We come now to other countries with approximately the same rate. There is Northern Ireland at 45; Scotland, 45; Eire, 49; and then, down at the bottom of the list, Roumania with 199.

Supply-Health and Welfare
There is one notable feature in connection with this comparison of rates. We look to the United States with its large coloured population, as well as a large population in cities, in which there are slums. It has a rate of 32, as compared with our rate of 44. This gives us something to think about, I suggest. It gives us something to shoot at. In spite of the fact that we are doing what we can in this country, and that our rate is steadily dropping, this difference of 12 points over the United States rate is worth considering, because it shows that we must be lax in some way, when we compare the figure for this country with that of the great country to the south.
There are certain things that come to our notice when we consider causes of death in infantile mortality rates. Communicable diseases have been dropping steadily. The loss rate in 1948 was 815. Pneumonia remains about the same, with 2,220 children dying in that year from pneumonia and bronchitis.
But there is one other disease which stares us in the face, showing a casualty rate of 1,472 from diarrhoea and enteritis. Perhaps that might be improved as we proceed with our program of better water supplies, pasteurization and better sanitation. I feel more could be done in the matter of premature births, because there we had a casualty list of 3,892 in 1948. But from all causes-and I have not included some of the others- we have an infantile deaths casualty list of 15,164 in Canada.
I remember stating before, and I state again, that I think many of these children- and we shall refer to them as babies, because most of them were in their first year of life-could have been saved. Quite a large percentage could have been saved, and no doubt will be saved as we proceed with our program.
It is interesting to note the improvement shown in the past 25 years. Of the children born between 1944 and 1948, approximately 72,000 who would have died at the rate prevailing between 1926 and 1930 lived to their first birthday. So I feel we can go ahead with our program, although not feeling satisfied with it, because there is room for great improvement. We bring people into this country. As I remember stating once before, if the 15,164 children could be saved they would be the best immigrants we could bring to this country.
Mental diseases continue on the upgrade so far as numbers are concerned. It is rather disturbing to note that on December 31, 1948, we had 55,858 people confined to mental institutions. I think in this program we could save many of those people

before they ever get to the institutions. There was a time when mental institutions simply gave custodial care, but now a large percentage of those who enter are coming out cured. With the program carried on in the schools and mental health clinics it is possible that many of those people would never reach the stage where they would have to go into institutions.
Again it is alarming that, even though our population is increasing, mental disease seems to be increasing at a faster rate. Our great neighbour to the south gave some alarming statistics at the time of the examination of their recruits. It disclosed that the number of young men being refused entrance into the army because of nervous and mental conditions is alarming. I hope that the same condition will not be found to exist in Canada in case there is a general call to the colours in the event of war. There is a great lack of trained psychiatrists in Canada. I would hope that more of the young men graduating would enter this field, because there is a great need for their services in order to cut down the alarming increase in patients entering our hospitals suffering from mental diseases.
I come now to the matter of hospital beds. Due to the program of grants for hospital beds, inaugurated by the province of Ontario, as well as the assistance given by the dominion government for the same purpose, many new beds have been added but there is still a grave shortage in almost every hospital. There is also a great shortage of nurses, and some program should be arranged to attract more young women to the nursing profession. If the profession were made more attractive I am sure many more young women would enter training. You cannot operate hospital beds without nurses. More nurses will be required for mental and other specialized hospitals, as well as in industry. As we go on increasing services of this type there will be a greater demand for nurses.
Hospital executives are finding increasing difficulty in maintaining their institutions. There was a time when hospitals depended upon donations and fees received from patients, and were regarded as institutions supported by philanthropy. Our health plans are broadening out and we are bettering conditions in Canada. The time has come when hospitals should receive more aid from the provincial and federal governments. We have reached a period when they must be regarded as a public utility. It has always been amazing to me that suffering and misery should be considered as something to be alleviated mainly by philanthropy or grants.

Hospital boards are mainly in the red so far as their finances are concerned. They are running behind each year, and finding it increasingly difficult to keep their institutions on an even keel. Hospital executives feel that it will create a bad impression if they keep on raising fees. That just cannot be done. Fees have had to be raised, and in doing this the cost of sickness has been placed far beyond the means of the average man. Quite often a man on a moderate salary has illness in his family requiring a long period of hospitalization, and he soon finds himself in a financial position from which it is pretty hard to recover. Something will have to be done to maintain our hospitals, and I tie in with that the high cost of hospitalization. We must continue to try to reduce our mortality rate. If we are to reduce our infant mortality rate it should be made possible for people to enter hospitals at rates they can afford to pay. These costs are rapidly getting beyond the power of the average person to pay.
This committee should consider seriously the position in which our hospitals are at the present time in spite of the grants given by the federal government and by some of the provinces, including my own province of Ontario. But every province in Canada is not in the same position and we must realize that any citizen of Canada, no matter in what province he lives, is as important to the whole of Canada as the citizen living in a province which has the financial ability to carry out certain health plans.
This is a most important matter. I find these mortality rates most appalling, and we should do more about them. We should institute a program; and in considering that program more time should be given by this committee, instead of passing these items in just a few hours at every session of parliament.
I mentioned one matter which I said did not come within the realm of the minister's portfolio, our high accident rate; but we also have very high infant mortality rates. Many young citizens are being lost to our great dominion. These are matters in which this committee should be greatly interested. When an accident occurs a coroner's inquest is held and the matter is thoroughly investigated, but the fact that so many babies die during the first year of life is something far more important and should receive much more consideration.
Hon. members can find the various mortality lists in the Canada Year Book. They will find the rates for the various diseases and how the different areas are affected.
Supply-Health and Welfare Without naming any particular province, there are some which are somewhat-I do not like to use this word-backward and whose mortality rates are higher than others. A citizen in any province in Canada is just as important as any other citizen in any over-all plan.
There are special cases in connection with which I should like to make an appeal. For years I have talked about arthritis, but new groups are coming forward for various diseases which require special attention. One which is seemingly becoming more prevalent is disseminated sclerosis. I receive a great many letters on this matter. I know plans are being made by people who are interested, to do something about this dread disease. I received an invitation the other day to attend a meeting in Ottawa to discuss this matter. We are gradually becoming aware of the number of people Who are suffering from this condition.
I am also interested in the rehabilitation of the victims of infantile paralysis. We have not yet found a cure for infantile paralysis, but I am proud of the efforts being made by the province of Ontario to rehabilitate the victims of this disease. Every child suffering from infantile paralysis is sent into an approved hospital where there are members of the staff trained in the rehabilitation of these cases. It is simply amazing to see these cases when they go into some of the hospitals-the Ottawa Civic hospital is one that is doing a splendid job-and when they come out. It is interesting to see a child go in with a very marked paralysis and come out some months later with no visible signs of paralysis. If this plan could be carried out in all the provinces of Canada it would prevent a great deal of crippling of little children who are afflicted with this dread disease. I am proud of the efforts made by -the province of Ontario, but possibly other provinces are not as financially able to assist. I think statistics will bear out that the way the province of Ontario has handled this disease has been most worthy and has prevented a great deal of crippling. All expenses of the patient are paid. The province pays the cost of all hospitalization and specialized treatment up to the point where patients have gone as far toward recovery as they possibly can. Then they are treated later at outdoor clinics. Instructions are given to parents on how to carry on massage and various exercises.
If this program could be put into effect all across Canada I am perfectly sure we could rehabilitate many of these children and restore them to perfect health. I remember the old days when we had nothing whatever

Supply-Health and Welfare to offer. We used to try some massage after the acute part of the disease had passed away, and we had many cripples. I have seen cases nowadays come out with no apparent paralysis and make a complete recovery. Before this program was instituted I am sure they would have been crippled.
I mentioned before the dinner hour the matter of coronary thrombosis, and that brings me to the question of research. The high rate of casualties in cancer, tuberculosis, coronary thrombosis and other heart diseases demands that we along with other countries keep up our research. We have a brilliant record in the Dominion of Canada in the field of research. Our scientists have contributed a great deal to the cure of certain diseases that were formerly thought to be hopeless. I think we should do our share in the granting of money for research in such diseases, and especially the ones I have mentioned, coronary thrombosis and arteriosclerosis. Every day the problem of coronary thrombosis is before us.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to mention in passing that so far as all these matters are concerned, research funds have been made available, as my hon. friend knows, out of the grant.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am aware that research funds have been granted, but I am calling for more and more research to help Canadians who suffer from these conditions. So far as coronary thrombosis is concerned, there is not a day when we are not made aware of this disease having affected people in our circle of friends or prominent men in the life of the country. There must be a cause. There must be something we can do in order to halt the increase in the number of people who are being carried off by this disease.
I come now to the problem of our aged people. It is true that under legislation passed by this parliament the old age pension came into effect. It is doing a wonderful job so far as helping our aged citizens is concerned, but when they become disabled sometimes it is difficult to find places for them. They become chronically ill or are considered ill by reason of their age, and we find them in public hospitals and institutions, places where they really should not be.
I think the time is coming when we will have to give more thorough consideration to the building of hospitals for those who are chronically ill, and especially for our aged citizens.
Some organizations are doing work along the line of propaganda of a type that warns people about the danger of certain of the diseases I have mentioned. I do not mean the type of propaganda you sometimes hear


on the radio or see in the press that really frightens people. The desire is not to frighten people but to make them more aware of their own physical condition so they will take an interest. This applies principally to the early diagnosis of cancer, and it might apply to tuberculosis. Even in the province of Ontario, where we have mass X-rays and mobile X-ray clinics, it is sometimes difficult to get the odd person to have an X-ray. They say they are afraid that something might be found. That is the reason they do not want to have a chest X-ray. These are all things that I suggest to the committee we should carry out. It is a mark to shoot at. We should try to cut down the incidence of these diseases, to cut down, as we have been doing, the incidence of infantile mortality. Cut down the rate of maternal mortality. Keep up the good work we have been doing in tuberculosis, and above all let us have research into some of these diseases whose cause and cure are unknown.
That should be the basis of any health plan in the Dominion of Canada. We should establish new forms of treatment that would be available for every citizen. We should make the opportunity for treatment available to every citizen. I place these matters before the committee knowing that the committee is sympathetic. Again I voice the opinion that it is unfortunate that a committee of the house could not be allowed to help the department by considering what more could be done to cut down the incidence of diseases and the mortality rate.
