speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, members in all parts of the house will agree that one of the greatest disappointments at this session of parliament is the failure of the government to take any steps in connection with the establishment of a nation-wide program of health insurance. As the committee knows, in June, 1951, the Minister of National Health and Welfare indicated to us that it was his hope that at the 1952 session of parliament we would have a special committee to study

all aspects of health insurance. There have been many examples of committees of the house which have been simply a means of delaying action, but some of us hoped that a committee on health insurance would not fall into that category. The reason we dared have that hope was because of the success that resulted from a similar committee in 1950 on old age security. Indeed I think it is fair to say that the idea of having a special committee on health insurance was born in that committee on old age security. The terms of reference of that committee in 1950 limited us to the subject of old age security, but other matters in the field of social legislation were constantly impressed upon us as requiring attention. One of them was the need for health insurance. I am sure it is correct for me to say that the members of that committee on old age security felt that it would be most useful if, with the least possible delay, we could have had a similar committee on health insurance.
It was, therefore, a matter of keen disappointment, which I am sure has been felt not only on this side of the house but by many members on the government side, when during the first week of this session the Minister of National Health and Welfare in answering one of my questions indicated that the government had decided there was to be no committee on health insurance at this session of parliament. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I take the opportunity in this general discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare to impress upon the minister, and through him the government, the urgent and crying need for health insurance for the people of this country. Not only is it an urgent need; it is a subject about which a great deal has been said, written, and studied across many years. In fact, Mr. Chairman, a good deal of politics has been played with this question of health insurance, dating right back to 1919. In August of that year the Liberal party held its last national convention but one, and included in its platform a pledge to bring in health insurance, along with certain other items.
That was 33 years ago, and we are still waiting for the implementation of that promise. The greatest amount of activity with regard to health insurance, at least in terms of talk by the Liberal party, took place in the forties, particularly in the early forties during the second world war. For example, in the speech from the throne that was read on January 28, 1943, as recorded at page 2 of Hansard for that year, there is this paragraph:
My ministers believe that a comprehensive national scheme of social insurance should be
Supply-Health and Welfare worked out at once which will constitute a charter of social security for the whole of Canada.
The government-
That was the Liberal government which we still have with us.
-accordingly proposes to recommend the early appointment of a select committee to examine and report on the most practicable measures of social insurance, and the steps which will be required to ensure their inclusion in a national plan. Among matters which will be referred to this committee for study and consideration will be the establishment of a national system of health insurance.
That was in January, 1943. If one looks at the speech from the throne in January, 1944, we find the promise repeated again in these words taken from page 2 of Hansard for that year:
When suitable agreements are reached with the provinces, my ministers will be prepared to recommend measures to provide for federal assistance in a nation-wide system of health insurance . . .
Now, Mr. Chairman, during those years 1943 and 1944 a number of other things were done. We have, for example, the Marsh report. The official title is "Social security for Canada, prepared by Dr. L. C. Marsh for the advisory committee on reconstruction". Hon. members will recall that this was at the time of the well-known Beveridge report in the United Kingdom, and it seems that the government here felt it should match the Beveridge report. So Dr. Marsh was called upon to produce this report on rather short order, and it was made available to the special committee on social security which met in 1943. It has a number of pages dealing with the question of health insurance and urging the importance of early enactment of legislation in that field.
We also had in that same session of 1943 this voluminous book entitled "Health insurance-report of the advisory committee on health insurance, appointed under order in council P.C. 836, dated February 5, 1942." It contains a mass of information about matters related to health in Canada and other countries; and it also contains a draft bill for health insurance in Canada which later was incorporated in the report of a special committee of this house, which was tabled in the house and which may be found in the Journals of the session of 1944.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, during these years as evidenced by the speeches from the throne, and as these documents show, a great deal of attention was being given to the question of health insurance, and the people of Canada were led to believe that a nationwide health insurance program was just around the corner.
We had these moves in the direction of health insurance not only here in the House of Commons. A resolution on the matter was

Supply-Health and Welfare passed by the national Liberal federation in September, 1943, which read in these terms:
The Liberal federation commends the government . . . for the steps already taken to prepare the way for a comprehensive system of health insurance and recommends inclusion of health insurance in a nation-wide scheme of social insurance.
Well, Mr. Chairman, despite all this activity -this printing of books and preparing of reports and a draft bill-nothing was done. The draft bill was never introduced in the house and certain questions which I asked this year would seem to indicate it has gathered considerable dust since that time.
The next important step in this direction came in 1945, when the dominion-provincial conference met after the election of that year. Hon. members will recall that very prominent among the proposals of the government of Canada to the governments of the provinces were proposals for health insurance. These proposals appear on pages 28 to 31 of the green book entitled "Proposals of the government of Canada". There are a few paragraphs from these proposals which I feel I should put on the record. I am quoting from page 29:
Health insurance has been widely adopted because it is regarded as the best means of meeting and of distributing fairly the costs of illness and, in conjunction with preventive services, of improving the general health of the nation. Specifically:
(1)	Health insurance enables the cost of illness to be prepaid, so that by paying regular sums when they are well people are able to meet the costs of illness when they are ill without being financially crippled.
(2)	Health insurance not only enables individuals to prepay their medical costs, but does this in such a way as to secure a wide pooling of risks and distribution of costs in much the same manner as any other form of insurance.
(3)	The provision of funds by all persons within a large area makes it possible for hospital and medical services to people in that area to be planned and administered more efficiently and economically than could be done by any other method.
(4)	The provision of better facilities for treatment and advice also operates to reduce the total incidence of disease and preventable death. Health insurance must be accompanied by adequate public health measures of a preventive character, but health insurance itself also provides important preventive benefits.
(5)	Health insurance permits the steady extension of health services into areas not previously covered, and the rapid application everywhere of new methods and services as they are discovered and developed.
I am putting that section of the federal government's proposals on the record at this time not only to indicate the very close and detailed attention which was given to the problem before these proposals were made, but also to point out that despite the argument that is sometimes used that we must get our health facilities first and wait until after that before we establish health insurance, it was contended in the paragraphs I just

read that the establishment of health insurance actually facilitates the development of the health services that are necessary to a complete program. That is our contention.
I cite as another example what has happened because of Blue Cross and similar types of programs. The very fact that they have come into being, the very fact it has been possible for many more people than was formerly the case to have hospital care, has played a part in creating a greater demand for hospital beds and has helped facilitate the development of health services,
The Liberal government has continued to talk about health insurance; yet that set of proposals was made nearly seven years ago and we still do not have a health insurance program. The proposals in 1945 were spelled out in considerable detail, and the amount of money involved was worked out. The government was prepared, in fact, to put the sum of $150 million into health insurance. That was the federal government's proposal in 1945.
I know we have had a good many arguments as to who was to blame for the break-up of the 1945 conference. Every time we raise some of these points it is suggested that that is the reason these matters have not been proceeded with. I would point out that some of the things that were proposed in 1945 have been implemented since, even though it took a great deal of activity from this side of the house, such as the removal of the means test from the old age pension. It is also true that despite the fact that an overall agreement regarding taxation matters between the federal and provincial governments has not been achieved, agreements with eight of the individual provinces have been made. In my view the break-up of the conference is no excuse for the federal government having failed to go ahead with the nation-wide program of health insurance.
Subsequent to these proposals, every time we have raised these matters we have had some sort of promise from the government to the effect that it was still its intention to bring in health insurance when it could. For example, during the debate on the minister's estimates in the session of 1947, as found in Hansard for June 20 of that year, some of of us raised the question as to why we were not making more progress with respect to health insurance. The minister said, as recorded at page 4423:
I can only repeat that we are engaging the full time of at least six persons in the department with four additional persons who have other duties to perform. When we have the type of conference with the provinces which we envisage we shall be prepared at that conference to submit details in respect to the studies we have been making and

are making and to bring about at the earliest possible moment the realization of a health insurance scheme.
I point out that in those promises that have been repeated time and time again, reference has been made not just to the health grants about which the government boasts so much, but specific reference was made to a nationwide program of health insurance as part of a nation-wide program of social insurance. Yet despite these repeated promises we still have no program of health insurance for the people of Canada.
Some members in this house will remember the day in May, 1948, when the late Mr. King, as prime minister, announced the health grants program. He told us then very clearly, and it has been stated to us since, that that program was to be the foundation of an over-all program of health insurance. We welcomed and applauded the announcement Mr. King made that day, even though we recognized that we were getting just twenty cents on the dollar so far as the 1945 proposals were concerned, as contained in the green book from which I quoted a few minutes ago.
I have in my hand a copy of the front page of a newspaper that is not unfriendly to the Liberal government, the Toronto Daily Star of May 15, 1948.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: An independent newspaper.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I missed that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I said "an independent newspaper".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Do you wish it were?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I hear Liberals on the other side say they wished this paper did not support them quite as much as it does.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That was a Flemingism you heard.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
At any rate, this newspaper's attitude toward Mr. King's announcement of May, 1948 was characterized by this banner headline, "Can't Wait for Ontario-King" Another heading: "Delayed health plan as long as we could for Ontario-Mr. King". Another heading: "New plan gives every individual Canadian ticket to healthy life". As one reads the articles by Borden Spears and Robert Taylor on the front page of this newspaper it is clear that these correspondents for the Toronto Daily Star thought this announcement of Mr. King's really envisaged health insurance as just around the corner. In fact they even got a bit political about it in a story down in the lower left-hand corner which is headlined, "Plan seen '49 vote move; C.C.F., Tories embarrassed". This was a story which suggested that the purpose of Mr. King's announcement was to steal the
Supply-Health and Welfare platforms of other parties, and that this announcement that health insurance was just around the corner would do the trick in the 1949 election. Well, Mr. Chairman, maybe it did the trick in the election, but the people are beginning to think it was a trick because there is still no health insurance, despite the great ado that was made at that time over the health grants program.
I repeat that we welcomed that program with enthusiasm. We are delighted with what has been done under it, but it is just twenty per cent of what was promised in 1945, and there has been no implementation of the promise that we would have health insurance.
I move on to Hansard for June 20, 1950. This was another occasion when we were debating health insurance on the present minister's estimates. He gave us another of those assurances that we are going to get there some day. These were his words on June 20, 1950, as found at page 3906 of Hansard for that year:
We are making most careful studies of this whole problem. We are waiting now for the results of the important surveys that are being conducted by every one of the provincial governments. The cost figures that will come out of those surveys are an integral part of anything that might be done. I want to assure my friend that we are making most serious studies. As he knows, we have brought into the department a number of individuals, one of whom has had previous experience in the matter of health insurance with one of the provinces. We are constantly encouraging, through that division and through our research division, a most careful study of this matter.
I am sure if I had not told the minister those were his words, he would have recognized them. They are the sort of words he has given us so often: The matter is being studied, or it is being given careful consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Good thoughts expressed in elegant language.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, good thoughts expressed in elegant language, but still no health insurance; and that despite the fact that it has been a good thought expressed in elegant language ever since 1919. We are kept waiting for the election after the next. That seems to be the Liberal slogan: The election after the next we will win on health insurance. I can tell the government that some day the trick will be turned.
In the same year from which I have just quoted some of the minister's elegant words we had the tabling of the report of the special committee on old age security. I have already indicated that, despite the fact that its terms of reference were limited to old age security, we found it impossible in that committee to refrain from discussing

Supply-Health and Welfare a number of other related questions. In fact we not only discussed them; we made reference to them in our report. For example, on pages 103 and 104 of that report we had a section entitled "Other Claims to Priority", and there are several paragraphs which speak of the fact that old age security has to be looked at in relation to the total problem of social security. One of the other problems which we said was most important was that of health insurance. For example, let me read paragraph 25 at page 104:
Nor has the committee overlooked other social security programs which have been widely advocated such as health insurance, invalidity pensions, etc. These are not, of course, matters which come within the committee's terms of reference. Furthermore, the committee has not been able to obtain precise data which would enable it to assess accurately the magnitude of the cost of programs of this nature. It has been estimated, however, that the over-all cost of a comprehensive system of health insurance would probably be not less than $300 million annually, although it must be added that a large proportion of such an amount would represent not a new burden on the people of Canada, but merely a rechannelling of existing expenditures on various forms of health care.
I have read that paragraph and I referred to what went on in that committee to indicate that in the committee on old age security we gave thought to this question of health insurance and made references to it in our report, which was unanimous. I repeat what I said a moment ago, namely that I am sure most if not all of those who were on that committee thought it would not be long until we obtained a similar committee to go into this whole question of health insurance. Some of us kept asking for that committee, and finally on June 21, 1951, as recorded in Hansard at page 4462, the minister intervened in a debate which, under two or three headings, had been going on for three days in relation to this question of health insurance, and this is what he said:
We will examine that problem,-
The reference is to health insurance.
-and in the regular session of 1952 I hope that we may be able-and I think I may go further than that and say that we are giving consideration to the matter-to set up a parliamentary committee to examine this whole problem.
I recognize the fact that what the minister said there was in two parts. He did not say categorically, "We shall have the committee"; but he did say categorically, "I hope that we may be able to set up a parliamentary committee to examine this whole problem."

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No; I did not say that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Just a minute. I read the whole of the sentence first; and then to make clear that the minister was saying two 
things, I left out in what I just said- but I intend to bring it in now-the part between the dashes; in other words, the part in parenthesis. The minister expressed his hope that we might have the committee. That was one statement. The other was in parenthesis when he said:
-and1 I think I may go further than that and say that we are giving consideration to the matter-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In order that the matter will be correctly stated, may I say this. I know what my hon. friend's argument is going to-be. That statement is clear. What I said there was that I hoped we would be able to-give consideration to the setting up of a committee. The words are clear. We have given the matter consideration, and I have given the reasons it has not been set up. My hon. friend must not say the words mean something that I did not intend them to-mean.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have the floor. I do not want this to go further without getting on the record precisely what the minister said. He did not say that he hoped to give consideration to the matter. He said he hoped we would have the committee and in parenthesis he said that they would give consideration to the matter. Let me put the statement on the record again, direct from Hansard, in his own words, including the part that is there between the dashes:
We will examine that problem, and in the regular session of 1952 I hope that we may be able-and I think I may go further than that and say that we are giving consideration to the matter-to set up a parliamentary committee to examine this whole problem.
Mr. Chairman, the -country thought that was what was going to happen. Indeed, those of us who have been disappointed by many committees in the past dared to hope that the work of that committee would result in steps in the direction of health insurance, even as the committee on old age security resulted in positive steps in the direction of new old age pension legislation. Hon. members know that when we arrived back here this year, on Friday, February 29, 1952, as recorded at page 18 of Hansard, I asked this question of the minister:
Will the special parliamentary committee on. health insurance, which the minister on June 21 last said he hoped to set up at this session, be established at an early date?
The minister's reply was:
My hon. friend did not give me the usual notice,, and possibly on that account my answer will not be as complete as it otherwise would be.
There is an interjection of mine to the effect that he had had eight months to think about it, and then the minister said:
I did say, as my hon. friend said in part, that the government would give consideration to the-

setting up of such a committee. The hon. member did not use those words when he put his question to me. The government has given careful consideration to this matter and has come to the conclusion not to set up such a committee at this time.
Mr. Chairman, I regarded that statement- as I am sure many hon. members of the house did, including members on the government side-as one of the most disappointing replies we have had to questions on the orders of the day, for we had counted on that committee.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The hon. member is wound up tonight.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what is the situation at the present time? Support for health insurance is growing in many parts of this country. For example, everyone recalls the strong support it was given last fall all over this province of Ontario by the then leader of the provincial Liberal party, one Walter Thomson.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: He was a good man.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: A fine boy. He was the best friend we ever had.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: He was the best friend the Conservatives ever had.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I hope you can keep him going.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The shades may come down on you too.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I hope you do not forget that I am the one who has the floor. We now have Mr. Lapalme, the Liberal leader in the province of Quebec, coming out with a Liberal program for that province. It was published in a striking advertisement in the Montreal Gazette of Tuesday, June 3, 1952, at page 21. He has eight points against Duplessis and eleven points for himself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It will not be enough for him to win.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Point No. 7 for Mr. Lapalme, the Liberal leader, is health insurance. It is short, but there it is. So we have the Liberal party in Ontario and the Liberal party in the province of Quebec both committed to programs of health insurance.
In addition we have had a number of provincial health surveys tabled by the minister during the last few weeks. A number of them have gone the other way but two in particular-one from Saskatchewan and one from Alberta-have strongly recommended a nation-wide program of health insurance, with provision for provincial participation as fast as individual provinces wish to participate in such a plan. I strongly urge upon the government that consideration be given to just such
Supply-Health and Welfare a plan of operation, and that there be no further delay in going ahead with this matter.
As the minister knows, a number of questions about this subject have been placed on the order paper at this session, a number of them in my name and some in the names of other members. From the answers to those questions we have obtained a good deal of information. Some of the sessional papers were tabled just today; hence I have not had time to collate all the information contained in them, but that information is extremely interesting and significant. I find, for example, that a very large number of people are already covered to some extent under Blue Cross and provincial schemes, which makes it clear that it would not be breaking brand new ground, not launching into a field in which nothing is being done, to go into a nationwide program of health insurance. It is simply a case of expanding upon something we now have, expanding upon a principle that has been proven to be worth while, and making it available to all Canadians regardless of their individual financial position.
It has now come to our knowledge that the minister's department apparently expected a committee, and has done a great deal of work upon it. I have on my desk two monographs from the research division of the Department of National Health and Welfare, one of which is entitled "Health Insurance in Sweden", social security series memorandum No. 10. The other is "Health Insurance in Denmark", social security memorandum No. 9, revised. On the back cover page of each of these memoranda I find a list of some 15 documents which have been prepared. They include social security legislation and old age legislation in various countries; and they also include health insurance legislation in those countries, plus surveys of physicians and dentists in Canada.
One of the points which interests me is that these booklets are prepared in precisely the same form as were the booklets prepared for our old age security committee by the same research division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. This suggests to me that the officials in the minister's department not only expected the committee, but are ready for a study of health insurance to be made by members of the House of Commons. In fact one of the sessional papers, No. 85A, tabled on Monday, April 7, 1952, in response to questions of mine, indicates that the Department of National Health and Welfare has considerable information on this whole question.
I also asked at that time this question: "Has there been consultation with the provinces

Supply-Health and Welfare concerning a program of health insurance?" The answer to that was:
Yes, at each meeting of the dominion council of health composed of the federal and provincial deputy ministers of health.
Thus the documents I have referred to, which have been prepared in the minister's department, and the answers in these various sessional papers on my desk all show quite clearly that the department has done a great deal of work on the question; and I commend the minister for that. There was a day when, on the item of health insurance studies, we criticized the minister strongly because he was not even using the money we were voting for this purpose. But now they are using it. They have done the studying. They have sent officials of the department to other countries. They know the story. They could call a committee together even now, before the end of this session, and lay a great deal of information and material before it which its members could study, and on the basis of which we could come to some conclusion.
I said a few moments ago that at least two of the provincial health survey reports have strongly recommended a nation-wide program of health insurance. For example, I hold in my hand a copy of the Saskatchewan health survey report, which was tabled by the minister not long ago. At pages 225 and 226 there are recommendations with respect to this question. It states:
Now that the health grants and especially the grant for hospital construction have paved the way for a health insurance program, there is no longer cause for further delay in bringing the benefits of health insurance to the people of Canada. It is recommended that:
The federal government should extend the scope of the national health grants program by adopting immediately a national health insurance program.
In the interests of assuring uniform benefits for all Canadians, a national health insurance system should be established with administration decentralized to regions corresponding to the several provinces or delegated to official provincial health agencies.
In the event it is decided that health insurance is to be organized and administered on a provincial rather than on a national level, the federal government should adopt immediately the provisions for a national health insurance program as contained in the proposals to the provinces in 1945. The federal government should establish basic standards to be met by the provinces as conditions for receiving the grants in order to provide at least minimum uniform benefits throughout all Canada, with reciprocity of benefits for insured persons moving from one province to another.
In connection with the suggestion made by the Saskatchewan health survey committee to the effect that if the federal government is not ready to launch a program immediately effective in the whole of Canada, at least they should launch the kind of program that would permit provincial participation, may I remind the government of

the stand Mr. Mackenzie King took on April 15, 1926, in relation to old age pensions which is similar to the stand we are asking the government to take now. On that day Mr. King, as reported at pages 2501 and 2502 of Hansard, had been asked by the Conservative opposition to have the old age pension bill delayed. This was the reply of the then prime minister:
The bill has been prepared with a view to avoiding delays and in order to enable any provincial government that may care to enact at once, with respect to old age pensions, legislation in conformity with the requirements of this measure to take advantage of the proposed scheme. If some provinces do not desire to pass such legislation, that determination will in no way affect the situation except in so far as they are concerned. But as a federal government we want to show our readiness at the earliest moment to assist any province as soon as it is prepared to enact legislation along the lines here laid down.
I am simply asking this Liberal government to take the same position with respect to health insurance that Mr. King took in 1926 with respect to old age pensions. His stand then was that if there was some province that did not wish to go ahead with old age pensions, that was not to be an excuse for denying old age pensions to people in provinces that were prepared to go ahead with it.
Today some of the provinces are ready to join with the federal government in the establishment of health insurance. I suggest the people of those provinces should not be asked to wait because some other provinces are not yet prepared. The time for action has come. A committee would not now be good enough; it is time for legislation. The time has come for the government to bring in a nation-wide program of health insurance. And in the light of the situation at the moment the most realistic and best scheme would be one that provides for provincial participation just as fast as individual provinces are prepared to participate.
I will let it go at that for the time being. The minister will hear more from some of us on this matter as time goes on, because we feel it is one of the most important questions before this country. We deplore the way in which politics has been played with this question since 1919. We deplore the continuing delay, the continuing refusal to deal with it. We would like to know what or who it is that stands in the way of action on this important question; and we urge the government to take action on it without delay.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? In the light of the present budget and defence expenditures, how would he propose financing it?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I hope the Minister of
National Revenue heard the paragraph I read from the report of the committee on old age security, which pointed out that a program of health insurance would be largely a rechannelling of the money that Canadians, either out of their own pockets or in groups, are already spending on health. The figures tabled today by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in response to my question show that as Canadians we are now spending on hospitalization and doctors' bills some $400 million. A health insurance program would not cost much more, if any more, than that sum of money. A health insurance program would be a means of rechannelling on a more sensible basis the efforts and money we are now expending so it would be spread over the entire community and so all Canadians would have the benefit of health care whether or not as individuals they could afford it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of going into a detailed survey of the health of the Canadian people, but I do want to say again that our people are the most important thing we have in this country. We should do everything possible to look after the health of our people, particularly in the way of research, as has been pointed out so well this afternoon and this evening. Research into cancer, tuberculosis and other diseases which are causing so many deaths each year should be carried on more extensively than is being done at the present time.
I want to renew my request to the minister to bring in legislation as soon as possible to take care of the physically incapacitated. Many of us who have the use of our limbs and senses find it difficult at times to make a living, and we should remember that those who are physically incapacitated find it most difficult to do so. Many of them are a heavy burden on their relatives and friends. I hope the minister will take cognizance of my request and, if not at this session, at least at the next session introduce legislation to provide pensions for these people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, the Liberal party have had health insurance in their platform ever since 1919. As far as I can see, and as far as the people in my riding to whom I have talked can see, we are just about as close to having health insurance today as we were 33 years ago.
Ever since 1919 the people of Canada have been promised before each election that they would have health insurance as a reward for voting Liberal. As soon as each election was 55704-186
Supply-Health and Welfare over, health insurance was wrapped up in mothballs and carefully put away until the next election.
As late as the recent by-elections we saw health insurance once again making its expected appearance. In the Toronto Daily Star of May 14 last we saw a large and handsome picture of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration posing with the Liberal candidate in Ontario riding, under the banner headline: "Foresees Health Insurance".
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, judging by the results in the by-elections the people are getting wise to what used to be evergreen bait. Perhaps it is losing some of its allure because it did not seem to have its usual resiliency in the byelections just over. It seems to me that whenever an election comes along the Liberal party look into the crystal ball. They see everything clearly, and there they see health insurance, no doubt about it. However, just as soon as the election is over, the crystal ball clouds up again, and health insurance fades into the distance.
Whenever the Minister of National Health and Welfare is asked when the government is going to bring in health insurance, he usually replies by alluding to the setting up of a committee to give the matter more study. I happened to be in Calgary last September when the minister was there, and though I did not see him personally, I read the report of his speech in the papers the next morning. According to the report, health insurance was going to be set up practically immediately. You could just see health insurance coming right along.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Has the hon. member my words there? I would like to hear them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have not, but they made an indelible impression upon my mind.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They were the minister's usual elegant words.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The government has in its possession all the information it needs to make a decision on this matter, and present a plan to parliament. In fact it has all the information that would be presented to a committee if one were set up. If a committee were set up, everyone knows that with its large Liberal majority, it would simply be a rubber stamp for the minister, and a time-consuming device to fill in the time between now and the next election. Then when that time arrived, we all know that health insurance would once again be used as election bait. If by some colossal mischance the Liberal party were again returned to power, it is just as certain as we are sitting here that

Supply-Health and Welfare health insurance would again be wrapped up in mothballs, and put away for another live years.
A question I want to ask, a question that the people I represent want to ask is this: Why is it necessary to carry on this prolonged double-dealing with the people of Canada on this vitally important matter? The people want health insurance, and the Canadian Medical Association is in favour of it, as evidenced by a statement of its president when speaking in Toronto on May 25 of last year. On that occasion the Canadian Press reported Dr. Gosse as follows:
He told the Ontario Medical Association that he favoured co-operation between citizens, doctors and government in developing health plans. He said the Canadian Medical Association believes citizens should pay their own contributions if able to do so, with governments bearing the cost for persons unable to contribute.
When speaking in the house last year, I stated that in my opinion the plan in operation in Great Britain would be unsatisfactory for this country. I then went on to outline the plan which had proved to be so successful in Sweden for the past 25 years and which I believed would do an excellent job in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend has referred to the Swedish scheme, and in order to know exactly what his position is I should like to know whether he is in favour of the new act in Sweden or the situation that has existed there for the last 23 years. Could he tell me which of the two schemes he favours? It would help me a great deal because I would like to compare what he has just said with statements that have been made by other members of his party with regard to this problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I believe in the scheme which has been in successful operation for the last 25 years, with any modifications which may have been brought in as improvements on the plan. I have talked both to doctors and patients from Sweden and they tell me they believe it is a very successful plan from all points of view.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The hon. member is not in favour of the new act?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am afraid I am not familiar with the new act. I am familiar with the plan which proved successful in that country for a period of 25 years. I think anything that is satisfactory for 25 years is a good plan. That does not say it cannot be improved. If it has been improved, then that is something again.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What is that plan?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The plan I suggested would not interfere with the present doctor-patient


relationship but would simply provide an easier method for people to pay their bills for the health services they receive.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Louder.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It calls for the patient to pay 25 per cent of the doctor, dentist or hospital bill with the remaining 75 per cent to be paid out of a health insurance fund maintained by regular contributions by all those who are financially able to contribute. The 25 per cent which is paid by the patient-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is just the other way around.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: -removes the something for nothing aspect of the British plan, which has caused those who do not actually need treatment to flock to the doctors' offices in Great Britain. They have done so in such large numbers that the treatment they can receive is, of necessity, superficial. On the other hand, the 25 per cent which the patient pays is not so much as to impose a severe financial' burden on the individual or on the family. It also ensures that the cost of the plan is kept to a minimum, because only those who actually need treatment apply for it. I ask the minister to say what he thinks of this plan or any modification of it. I am not an expert on health insurance. I am here to learn.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I will answer him right now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like the minister to answer when I am finished, and I will not be very long. I should like him to say what he thinks of the plan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not think very much of it, nor do very many people in Sweden.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like him to say what defects he thinks the plan possesses and how the plan can be improved. If he thinks this plan is of no use whatsoever, then I should like him to tell us what would be a better plan. That is what the people of Canada have been waiting to hear the minister and the government say for 33 years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What about the Tory government?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I think the answer is long overdue. The people of Canada have been waiting for a long time. I think it is about time the government told us what they have been thinking about for the past 33 years and what they think would be a good health insurance plan. Let them tell us about the health insurance plan they have been talking about before every election for the past 33 years, the health insurance plan they foresaw in the by-election campaign in the riding of Ontario and other ridings,

and in fact what is the plan about which they have been talking for a great many years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Give us your plan, George.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is always a pleasure to discuss the estimates of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I do not want him to interpret any remarks I make at this time as carping criticism. I think members of the house should keep most of the matters handled by the Department of National Health and Welfare out of the realm of politics. They are mostly humanitarian matters. There is lots of room for us to quarrel and be political on many other issues that come before the house. I know that as one member of the house I could not get up and criticize the minister personally for being uninterested. I have known him for a long time and, regardless of where he sits in the house, I think he is just as much interested as I am in any problem affecting the health of the people of Canada. He is moving slowly within the machinery with which he has to work. He is possibly going as fast as the many factors with which he has to contend will permit him. I would, always give him credit for being sincere in going as far and as fast as he can within these limitations. I say that because I know the minister pretty well personally.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
You are not a bad fellow
yourself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Do you fellows dance?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I like to pat on the back people who deserve it, and I love to kick people in the teeth when I think they deserve it. I did not like the speech made by my young and gallant friend from Broadview a few moments ago. I did not like it because first of all he said he believed in a national health insurance program, although he did not say exactly what he meant by that-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: He was talking through his false teeth.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
-and in the next breath he condemned Britain where they have implemented a national health insurance program. The program in that country is only in the experimental stage and a national health insurance program, like many other social problems with which you have to deal in life, is something you cannot finalize overnight. You cannot measure it in terms of days or years. When you are dealing with the problems of humanity in their various aspects, and health insurance is one of them, you are dealing with things that will be matters of trial and error for a long time. It will take a considerable time before you reach the 55704-1S6J
Supply-Health and Welfare point where you will get unanimity among the doctors, hospitals and patients and cooperation in all the machinery that has been built up in that field over the last 150 years.
It is not as easy as my hon. friend thinks to uproot one system overnight and transplant something else that is going to be 100 per cent perfect within a period of a year or two. I think my hon. friend was ill-advised to recommend that the Canadian government do something that is being torn to pieces slowly but surely by the Conservatives in Great Britain, and then suggest that he favours national health insurance. He cannot have it both ways. I am interested in this subject and I think the Department of National Health and Welfare is interested. I am not saying that in order to pat anyone on the back. I like to be honest about these things.
Within the last year the Department of National Health and Welfare asked the different provinces to make surveys of their ability at this time to handle a national health insurance program, because under our constitution the field of health is a provincial responsibility. Such surveys were conducted. Only two provinces in Canada said they wanted a national health insurance program, and they were named by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. They are the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. I did not pay very much attention to the surveys made in the other provinces but I did read the report of the survey made in the province of Nova Scotia which was tabled a week or so ago. In the final summary of that report they recommend against the adoption of a national health insurance program at this time. Some 28 reasons are enumerated as to why a national health program could not be implemented now.
I do not agree with that report. I do not agree with the summing up; because if the report made by the province of Nova Scotia indicated anything it indicated the complete inability of that province to cope with their health problem with their present finances and within the constitutional limitations, inasmuch as health comes within provincial jurisdiction.
Health has been a problem for the provinces since confederation, since 1867. Since that time the provinces have worked on a solution for that problem and the report I read from Nova Scotia proved conclusively, to my mind, that they have accumulated disabilities such as inadequacy of hospitals, lack of trained personnel, and lack of research facilities. Those disabilities have accumulated since confederation under the management of the provinces and, instead of indicating that
2954	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare a national health program is not advisable at this time, it proves conclusively that the provinces are not able to handle the problem.
I believe the only solution is an over-all health insurance program by the federal government on a contributory basis with the country zoned so that proper facilities may be set up. The continuation of what we have today places most of the people in this country in the position of not being able to take advantage of the medical skills and hospital facilities which are available because the cost is prohibitive.
I think that instead of accepting these reports the federal government should take a good look at them and decide that the time has come when the federal government must step into the field and clean up the disabilities which have accumulated under provincial management since confederation. I do not know all the details of the reports, but I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he says there is no reason now why two provinces, like Alberta and Saskatchewan who have done a good job and have to a large extent removed the difficulties that exist in some of the other provinces, as they are ready to take part in a national health program, should not be able to meet with the federal government to work out an agreement and establish a health program. In my opinion that would be setting a basis for other provinces to "come in when you can". If you started to work with the two provinces that are ready and arranged your financing that would be, in my opinion, a lead to other provinces in perhaps a year or so to also come in and work the thing out on a national basis.
I know that the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia are trying to work the matter out on a provincial scale. I am sure anyone who has watched the development of the provincial health program in any of those provinces would come to the conclusion that there is no solution on a provincial scale. Saskatchewan has done a good job with limited finances. I think they have gone perhaps as far as they can go. They have done an excellent job, and have provided pretty full coverage from the standpoint of hospitalization. They have set up their regions as an experiment and have covered their people for both doctor and hospitalization. They receive the co-operation of the medical people in that area and there is complete coverage for many specialized services, which are not available in other parts of the country under the local health schemes.
I know that the cost of doctor and hospitalization, under the panel system that has
[Mr. Gillis.1

been working in the part of the country I come from for a good many years, is just about five times as expensive annually as what they are doing in the province of Saskatchewan; and the plan I speak of has not nearly the coverage. I also know that hospitals in the area I speak of are getting into the position where they are continually stepping up the rates. They have more than doubled since 1939. Every time you pick up the paper the hospital board is going back to the subscribers asking for an increase in rates because the hospital is going in the hole and is being threatened with bankruptcy. In my opinion, instead of there being any improvement in the last ten years the services have been deteriorating and the costs have been mounting all the time.
Another thing is that every time you begin to talk about health insurance something else is born immediately. Personally I do not believe in the Blue Cross and all of these stopgap programs we have, because all they have succeeded in doing is preventing proper discussion and proper analysis of the whole problem of national health insurance. They are merely prolonging the agony.
The matter is a national one and it cannot be handled on any other than a national basis if it is to be financed and regulated properly. I have been convinced of that for a long time. I believe if this was done on a national scale and set up properly the cost per capita would be less than it is at the present time when we are trying to do it only in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan on a provincial basis. British Columbia has discovered that it is a pretty tough proposition, and perhaps one of the worst tangles they have on their hands in that province today is their provincial health program. I believe they got into a field they did not understand. They have not the finances, the personnel, or the facilities to handle the thing on a provincial scale. Alberta is doing fairly well, and Alberta and Saskatchewan are prepared to go ahead with a national plan.
When the minister is answering questions and criticism I would like him to comment on whether it is practical to do what was done with the old age pension originally; that is, to establish basic legislation so provinces which are in a position to come into this scheme may do so if and when they are ready. I think it is unfair, it is shortsighted, and it is bad organization for the federal government to take the position that two governments which are ready for something must stand out because seven or eight other provinces in the country are not ready.
There are just one or two other things by way of grievances which I would like to direct the minister's thoughts toward. One

is the matter of the old age security pension. When we took the means test out of old age security pensions we thought we had solved the situation. Like many cases, when you solve one problem you create three or four more. I am particularly concerned about the means test in two types of pensions. One is the blind pension.
The blind pension is paid because of disability. It is a separate act from the Old Age Security Act, but as soon as a blind person reaches age 70 he is immediately transferred from the blind pension to the old age security pension. In my opinion that is not right, and I do not think it would cost very much money to remove that very burdensome grievance.
My other point in connection with pensions to blind persons is that I believe the ceiling on permissible earnings is wrong. That ceiling is $600. I had thought it was always the policy of the department to encourage blind persons particularly to take some kind of occupation to interest themselves, instead of sitting around on pension brooding. Many of them are willing to occupy themselves, but they run into the problem of the ceiling on permissible earnings when they try to build up a little bit of a business. About all they can do is sell brooms or pencils, or operate a little canteen. Any time those earnings go over the $600 there is a deduction from the blind pension.
Those are the two complaints on the blind pension about which I should like the minister to do something. I believe it is wrong to pay the old age security pension and couple it with the blind pension, because the pensions are paid under two separate acts. The blind pension is paid for a disability, and when such a person reaches the age of 70 the disability is worse because there is infirmity along with it. If the person is lucky enough to be still alive at that stage, he is entitled to the old age security pension. I believe such a person should be paid the old age security pension without any reference to the few dollars he receives for his disability under the blind pension.
The next thing about which I wish to complain is coupled with the Pension Act. There is a type of pensioner, an old lady or an old gentleman who lost a son in the service who might have been the breadwinner at this time had he returned, who receives a pension of $40 a month. As soon as the pensioner reaches the age of 70 that dependent's pension is cut off by the Canadian pension commission. I realize that the means test is in the war veterans legislation, but I am just jogging the minister's memory about it. The Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Veterans Affairs are both members of the
Supply-Health and Welfare same cabinet. They should get together and remedy this situation. It is a rather sore spot, and I do not think very much money is involved. Either a blind person or an aged pensioner receiving that dependent's pension who reaches the age of 70 is not going to be here very much longer, and I think for the short period they are going to be around that means test should be removed. I am going to leave that thought with the minister. It is very difficult to make people understand why, after years of wrangling, the means test was removed from the old age pension and then have it immediately affect other pensions that had been in existence over a period of years.
I shall not take up more time, Mr. Chairman. I agree with what the member for Winnipeg North Centre had to say. He spoke at some considerable length and put all the facts and figures on the record. I believe he proved conclusively to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that the cost of an over-all health insurance program in this country today could be easily met out of the moneys that are already being spent in the field of health for hospitalization, doctors and so forth. There is another angle to this national health program which the hon. member for Broadview did not think about. While the health insurance program in Great Britain was on a contributory basis, it gave millions of people the right to a doctor and hospitalization which they had never had before because they could not afford it. Certainly in the experimental stages of the legislation mistakes were made. I never agreed with the idea of supplying wigs, false teeth, hearing aids and that sort of thing. I believe that was a premature step; but if the hon. member had stopped to think for a moment he would have realized that millions of people in Britain were provided with dental care who had never before had an opportunity to visit the dentist. There was a run on that sort of thing, and why would there not be? Those administering the health program were placed in a position where the results of fifty years of neglect in this field had to be cleaned up. Thousands and thousands of people made a run on this service because of those years of neglect. Perhaps such a run would last for three or four years, but after that condition was cleaned up the expenditures for this program would have been whittled down a great deal. Ultimately the program would have systematized itself.
I believe Mr. Churchill is doing the people of Britain a disservice by knocking off a lot of these health benefits. I believe he will re-create conditions which the Labour party was well on the way to cleaning up had they retained office long enough, or had the present

Supply-Health and Welfare government been wise enough to retain those benefits. While it may have appeared as though a considerable amount of money was being spent on the program, at the same time millions of pounds a year were being saved in other directions. How many of us stop to think about the tax we are paying at our door from week to week? Hardly a day goes by but what someone at the door is looking for a donation to the cancer fund, the Red Cross, the institute for the blind or the community chest. If you added up all the money you gave away at your door for health programs, which in my opinion is expended in a misdirected way, it would go a long way toward providing for health insurance. I believe a health program should be established in this country on the same basis as old age security, with a certain percentage of the taxes collected for that specific purpose. Then there would be no need for all this haphazard method of collecting money for health purposes. In my opinion money enough is provided to carry on research and set up clinics all across the country at which people could get proper examination and be directed to the proper treatment.
Mr. Chairman, that is all I have to say on the subject. I believe hon. members, regardless of where they are sitting, will realize that this question is not a political one so far as I am concerned. National defence is not a political question either. Whether or not my friends to the right think that I am justified in giving the minister a pat on the back, I believe any member who is honest will realize that since the establishment of that department under his direction we have taken many long steps forward in the field of social security in comparison to what we had at the time the department was formed. So far as I am concerned I am prepared to give credit where credit is due. I am not prepared at any time to play politics with the health of the people of this country. I believe that is the position of every member.
I am willing to kick the government around when it is necessary, but on this question I am willing to co-operate in any way I can in order to find a solution to this problem. Any time a member is in his riding, one of the most difficult problems facing him from day to day is the plea of the aged, or of crippled children, and the attempt to find some way by which hospitalization or treatment can be provided. I do not think that is good enough. I am prepared to support the government in anything they may o toward getting in this country a national health program on a contributory basis and keeping it out of the realm of politics.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

I propose to read a statement made b>
