maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in dealing with the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare I consider we are dealing with estimates which are as important as any we will find anywhere in this volume of estimates.
In looking over the figures for the current year one sees, using round figures only, that this year there will be spent through the department $734 million, which is the highest figure in the department's history. This compares with $479 million last year, or an increase over last year of $255 million. Practically all this sum is accounted for by increased payments on the welfare side of the department. New old age security payments will amount to $322 million; the federal government's half-share of old age assistance payments for those between 65 and 69 years will amount to $20 million, and the blind persons allowance will total $3 million, making a total of $345 million as compared

Supply-Health and Welfare with expenditures last year of $110 million for the old age pension then in effect. So on account of these payments for old age security, old age assistance and blind persons allowances there is an increase of $235 million in 1952 as compared with similar payments in 1951. Payments on account of family allowances are increased from $320 million to $332 million, due of course to increase in population. The remaining increase of $8 million is scattered through many items of the department. There are no significant increases this year in other items.	*
I am sure it does not require to be said again, because it is the view of all members in the house, that health is an asset. It is an asset not only to the individual who is fortunate enough to possess it, but it is an asset to the nation. Equally, ill health is a loss not only to the individual but to the nation as well.
On the welfare side of the work of this department, welfare payments are supported by all parties represented in the house, and I share the view expressed by the hon. member for Cape Breton South that these subjects are too important and mean too much to the people of this country to be made a matter of mere partisan exploitation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Listen to that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If you wish to get me started on that, I will have a good deal to say about it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You are doing all right as you are.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There are so many good ways of using money in connection with national health and national welfare that it seems to me we must be vigilant at all times as members of the House of Commons to assure ourselves that we are devoting to the very best possible use the money made available by parliament for expenditures on national health and national welfare.
There are so many things to be done that we are far from having reached the ultimate goals in either of these important fields. A number of the things lacking were mentioned this afternoon and this evening by my colleague the hon. member for Lanark in his very able speech. There is the field of preventive medicine, the need for research; and to this I would add the need in this country for a very great increase in hospital accommodation. There is still in all parts of Canada a very serious shortage of needed hospital accommodation. We cannot be content to rest, in view of the statistics available to us as to the national loss wrought by the scourge of disease.

From the daily bulletin of the dominion bureau of statistics of October 19 last I read this, concerning tuberculosis in Canada:
There was a slight increase in the number of tuberculous patients admitted to sanatoria and other hospitals which had facilities for their care and treatment in 1949, as compared with the preceding year . . . The total number of admissions during the year was 16,492 as compared with 16,326 in the preceding year. In 1949, 15,487 or 93-9 per cent of admissions were tuberculous as compared with 15,278 or 93-6 per cent in 1948. New cases admitted to sanatoria in 1949 numbered 9,340 as compared with 9,541, readmissions, reviews and transfers accounting for the remainder.
Then for the year 1950, from preliminary figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics, and which are to be found in the bulletin of the Canadian Tuberculosis Association for September and October last, we read that the rate of deaths per 100,000 from tuberculosis in 1950 for all of Canada was 25-9, and the provincial rates varied all the way from 13 in Ontario, which has the best record, to 68-5 in Newfoundland, a very startling figure.
Then there is the scourge of mental illness. In the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of March 10 last one reads this:
Both the number of admissions to Canadian mental institutions and the admission rates per 100,000 of the general population increased in 1949 and 1950 over the preceding year, while discharges also rose in number and rate per thousand patients, and deaths decreased in relation to number of patients, according to a preliminary report on mental institutions covering the years 1948 to 1950 released by the bureau.
The total number of admissions for all Canada increased from 14,184 in 1948 to 15,476 in 1949 and 16,377 in 1950, the rate per 100,000 of the estimated population rising successively from 110 to 114 and 118. Discharges in the three years numbered 9,952, 11,303, and 11,714, respectively, the rate per 1,000 patients moving upward from 144 in 1948 to 158 the following year and 159 in 1950.
Those figures as to admissions to mental institutions would unquestionably have increased if there were more accommodation available for patients in that category.
Then, too, it must be with a measure of disappointment, which all of us will share, that one reads reports like the one I find in the Globe and Mail of February 5, which reads:
Any suggestion that young people of today have better teeth than their parents would appear to be contradicted by the dental records of recruits now joining the Canadian Army.
Most of these recruits are in their twenties or late teens but nine out of ten of them need dental treatment of some kind, according to dental officers at defence headquarters here. The dental officers have been appalled at the general oral condition of the young men who have been enlisting since the start of the Korean war in the summer of 1950.
Then follows an extensive review of statistics on this subject. All Canadians are thankful for the progress that has been made

in combating the scourge of disease in Canada. But let no one think we have made such progress that we can afford, with smugness or self-satisfaction, to sit back and rest upon our oars. There is much work yet to be done in these two fields of vital importance, national health and national welfare. And it is because of the importance of these fields, and because there are so many ways in which assistance can be used to advantage, that it seems to me our duty is very high to continue at all times to use every means to improve governmental services, and to obtain always better value for the taxpayers' dollar.
That fact is impressed upon us all the more when we realize that the formula put forward by the Minister of Finance last October, the 2-2-2 formula, is not going to meet the cost of the new welfare payments. According to the Minister of Finance there is going to be in 1952 a deficit of $58 million on account of the new old age security and old age assistance payments.
Having regard to the factors I have mentioned I think we must search diligently in order to satisfy ourselves that the available funds for health and welfare are put to the best possible use. It was with not a little disappointment that in reviewing the figures of the details of this department I find that those two old items, travelling expenses and publicity, which have claimed so much of the money of the taxpayers in the past, seem to be still holding out their hands for more.
Travelling expenses this year for this department will total $1,023,700. I think in fairness there should be deducted from that at least a substantial part of the $300,000 item 271 earmarked for the transportation of patients and the travelling expenses of other than the staff. To the extent to which that sum provides for the transportation of patients and those travelling with them I am sure there will be no comment of disapproval. But even deducting all of that item we find that the total for travelling expenses for this department is $723,700.
Then there is the old and familiar item bearing the euphonious title of "educational and informational publications". I remember that item when it appeared under the simple title of "publicity". That did not appear to be a very popular title, particularly when it was found to cover some silly expenditures, and in later years it was given the more respectable title of "educational and informational publicity". Further respectability is now given to it by providing two new names. The first is "educational and informational 55704-187
Supply-Health and Welfare publications" and the other "educational and informational materials other than publications".
Whatever the appropriate name may be, the fact is that expenditures on that account in this department are going to total $707,920 this year. The two items of travelling expenses and publicity will require an expenditure this year in this one department of just about $1-5 million, apart from the item of $300,000 to which I made sympathetic reference.
Is an expenditure of those proportions necessary for the purposes of travelling and publicity? When we look at all the useful ways in which expenditures can be made to contribute directly to the improvement of the health of the nation it seems to me that to expend sums of those proportions upon travelling and-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question? When he was giving the information figure he may have noted that it includes a civil defence item. Apparently he has failed to note that there is actually a decrease in the item for information in connection with the normal activities of the department of health and welfare. I am sure he would want to make that very clear before the opposite impression got out.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am aware that on account of civil defence there are two items, one for educational and informational publications and the other for educational and informational materials other than publications, the amount being $108,500 in the former case and $204,500 in the latter. Taking account of those factors I am still submitting that too much money is being spent by this department upon travelling expenses and publicity, especially when we consider what the need is in this field of health and how the money could more usefully be spent in other ways.
As all of us who have reviewed government accounts well know, travelling is most expensive. If we had an adequate method of scrutinizing estimates in a select committee instead of this awkward and clumsy procedure in committee of supply, a committee of the whole house, there would be an opportunity of really sifting through these numerous items of travelling expenses and seeing just how much was really necessary and how much could be dispensed with without any effective loss in the administration of the particular department.
Not only do I think too much money is being spent on travelling and on publicity; I think some of the expenditures are unquestionably extravagant and wasteful in nature. Surely if money is going to be spent on

Supply-Health and Welfare publicity we want to see some return in useful instruction for our money. Let me consider some of the publicity issued by this department. Here is one rather colourful booklet entitled "Good Habits for Good Teeth". It shows a totem pole and an illustration of four little Indians polishing the teeth of the face on the totem pole. It contains six verses and is illustrated in various colourful ways, some of them amusing but none of them very dignified or I suggest very necessary. This piece of publicity like all the others bears the inscription, "Department of National Health and Welfare by authority of the minister Hon. Paul Martin."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Read it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Read the whole thing; it is very useful. I may tell the hon. member that the department of health in Ontario has ordered many copies of that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
May I tell the minister that many taxpayers in Canada can think of more useful ways of spending money than on that and some of the other issues that are coming out over his name and whose principal purpose apparently is to publicize the name of the minister.
Here is another one entitled "Industrial Health Bulletin." The February, 1951 issue contains a reproduction, extending over two pages, of an article on the subject of success in management. It goes on to enumerate eleven qualities which a successful executive will find useful. What on earth has that to do with national health? The minister is telling the people how they may become useful executives if they have:
1.	Achievement desires.
2.	The idea of authority.
3.	Strong mobility drive.
4.	Organizational ability.
5.	Decisiveness.
6.	Firmness of conviction.
7.	Activity and aggression.
8.	The need to overcome a sense of frustration.
9.	Realism.
10.	Relations with others.
11.	Attitude toward parents.
What on earth has all this to do with health?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The Ontario department of health has ordered many copies.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I come to a later issue of the same industrial health bulletin. This time it is the issue of March, 1952. It bears the caption, "Pictorial Presentation". The whole issue this time consists of twelve

cartoons which have been selected out of previous issues. In my submission there is nothing here that has anything to do with health, or with industrial health in particular. It is just a series of cartoons. They may be very amusing, but I do not think they are very amusing to the taxpayers who have to pay for them.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Have you ever heard the old saying, mens sana in corpore sano?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The purpose of the publication is to improve the minds and mental health of the people, and then bodily health will follow.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What a wonderful explanation! I am sure we listened with most rapt attention to that extraordinary justification, that apologia we heard from the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine. Look at what he calls that which contributes to a healthy mind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Here is one cartoon which shows a machine and the operator. It is a very big machine with a little wee operator beside it. The hon. member thinks such a cartoon will contribute to a healthy mind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to ask my hon. friend a question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then there is another cartoon with the note under it, "No caption was considered necessary for this illustration on employee relations". It shows-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member a question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Who has the floor?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend asked me-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Who has the floor?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: My hon. friend asked me a question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Order. The minister would like to ask a question of the hon. member but he cannot ask it unless the hon. member consents.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If it is only a question the minister wants to ask me I will certainly be glad to answer it, but I do not want him smuggling a speech into the middle of my remarks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The hon. member knows I would not do that. I understand my hon. friend has to leave tonight.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If my hon. friend were going to have to leave I was going to point out to him that no publication from this department goes out without a request coming first of all from one of the provincial departments of health in our ten provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there you have the minister's idea of what a question is. Where in that effusion from the minister do you find a question? I suggest that the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine ought to contribute some of his advice to the minister about a healthy mind. He might at least give the minister some instruction pertaining to a healthy mind on what a question is.
Again dealing with this particular publication which the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine thinks contributes so much to the healthy mind, here we have another cartoon in which an executive apparently is lifting a hangman's rope out of a suggestion box in the office, and we read that no caption was considered necessary for this illustration on employee relations. Then again there is a third cartoon with the caption: "Floor levels may be raised to compensate for the shorter height of women employees". We have an illustration of a movable part of the floor being lifted for the benefit of the female employee so she is at a proper height alongside her lathe.
The fourth cartoon is entitled, "Conference, do not disturb". It pictures five cavemen gathered around a table. One of them apparently has just been knocked out by a second one who holds a big club and the other three are holding their hands up. Has this anything to do with the nation's health, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It sounds like a Liberal caucus.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: So it goes. Here is another with a pretty nurse holding a workman's hand and it is called, "The nurse and the pulse of industry".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Oh, Paul, you can do better than that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Here we have another cartoon depicting a workshop with many workmen standing around watching and another who has a red paint pot in his hand is running for dear life with a bull after him. Is this a contribution to education in the view of the minister and the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine? Under the cartoon is the following:
This sketch, on colour in the plant, was entitled, "This always happens when he uses the red paint."
Supply-Health and Welfare
The taxpayers of Canada are paying to have that printed and circulated throughout Canada. Here is another one depicting a workman with a light finding another workman sitting in darkness with various machine parts scattered about, and we read this caption.
Illustrating an article on plant lighting conditions, this item was captioned: "Has anybody seen my lathe?"
Here is another showing the wreckage of an industrial plant and underneath it are these words:
The article was on industrial laboratories. The caption: "Our tests indicate a high explosive content in the sample."

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Don't you think that is pretty valuable?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I cannot see that it is valuable unless your mind is in such a condition that you think a statement, albeit a very extraordinary one, is a question, or unless you have the view of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine that these cartoons have the effect of creating a healthy mind. I can think of many better ways to expend the taxpayers' money in contributing to mental health than putting out cartoons of this kind. Mind you, I suppose everybody likes to see cartoons, but why at the expense of the taxpayers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You do not think they should do that?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not think you have any business wasting other people's money putting out things like that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then you disagree with the Canadian Congress of Labour.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I disagree with the minister or anybody else who says that particular issue, or issues of that kind, contribute anything to a healthy mind or a healthy body.
I note too that in the issue of the industrial health bulletin for February, 1951 the illustration of the successful executive who had those eleven useful attributes shows the executive holding a telephone receiver upside down because the cord is attached to that portion of the piece which is closest to his ear. Apparently he was talking into the receiving end of the set and listening through the speaking end.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: He is not the only one.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That represents the idea of the minister and the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine of what contributes to a healthy mind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
He is not the only one who is speaking through the wrong end.

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I am sure the minister likes company when he does not know the difference between a question and a statement, albeit a foolish one.
There is something that is common to all these publications. You know what it is, Mr. Chairman. You know well what it is, because they all bear the same so vital, so important inscription. Take the little booklet showing the Indians brushing the teeth on the totem pole. On it I read the following:
Department of National Health and Welfare by authority of the minister Hon. Paul Martin.
The last three words are in extra firm, clear and heavy type, "Hon. Paul Martin".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The workers' friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
You see, Mr. Chairman, the cheering section behind the minister is quite happy to see the money of the taxpayers of this country squandered on giving personal publicity to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
You know quite well, Mr. Chairman, the kind of inscription that appears on these industrial health bulletins to which I have made reference. It does not matter what other things are in them or left out of them as long as this very important statement is included, namely:
Published monthly for the industrial health division of the Department of National Health and Welfare, Ottawa, under the authority of the minister, the Hon. Paul Martin.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It does not matter what foolish squandering of the taxpayers' money the contents of the balance of the publication may represent as long as those essential words appear and are scattered throughout the length and breadth of Canada in all ten provinces. Of course one can say the more the better, according to the ideas prevailing on the other side of the house, as long as they contain these essential words, "The Hon. Paul Martin".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
That is what counts, Mr. Chairman, as you well know.
Now we know, of course, what the minister says every time people take issue with this silly squandering and improvident waste of the taxpayers' money. The minister gets up and, with his favorite lamentation, points to issues like "mother and child", and he just wracks our hearts as he pictures what is going to happen to the health of this nation if you cut out any of his precious publicity. The health of the nation is going to fall to pieces overnight unless he has his publicity going out.


Mr. Chairman, I think the minister has tried to scare the house often enough. Perhaps wie have come to the point where the boy sent to watch the flock has cried, "Wolf! Wolf!" often enough, and perhaps the house is not going to be quite so ready to be frightened this time if somebody tries to apply a little common sense and a sense of responsibility to wasteful expenditures of this kind.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I wish to touch for a moment on another subject of very considerable importance. This subject from time to time confronted the special committee which studied the subject of old age security at the 1950 session of this house. It was the problem of the disabled person. We were told the following year that a study was to be conducted, and I am hoping the minister will be able to make a report on this subject which will indicate that we are coming closer to dealing with this problem. I am referring to those persons who are totally and permanently disabled.
The house knows that at the recent session of the Ontario legislature an important step was taken in meeting this problem when provision was made for the payment of a monthly pension of $40 to persons in the province who are permanently and totally disabled and who are between 18 and 64 years of age. I suggest to the minister that there is a lead which can be commended in the recognition of the existence of a problem which has as much claim to consideration as other problems which have been dealt with. The house gave unanimous support to the legislation of a year ago dealing with the payment of pensions to the blind, as it had given strong support, unanimous support, to the previous provision that had been made for blind persons. Blindness is a particular form of disability. Mr. Chairman, by what logic do we differentiate between those on the one hand who are afflicted by blindness and those on the other hand who suffer permanent and total disability for other reasons? I submit there can be no distinction in logic in our approach to this problem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman permits? If I could not see you, I would be very unhappy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman for his very kind and generous comment. I can assure him it always gives me pleasure to look across to the other side of the house at him and, no matter what may be said for the rest of the scenery, as long as I can see him I feel happy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I will be your ghost writer.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the problem of providing for the total and permanently

disabled is one that is necessarily linked with the problem of rehabilitation. Here is a field in which much remains to be done. I am not suggesting that there has been in this respect a retardation of effort on the part of this department, because it is a field in which steps have to be taken in association with the province. I well recall the statement made by Dr. Davidson, in the committee on old age security two years ago, that a grant that had been made available for rehabilitation of the blind had not been fully taken up. However, Mr. Chairman, I have read with interest a statement attributed to the Minister of Labour at Montreal on March 6. A Canadian Press dispatch of that date reads:
More than 100,000 Canadians, men and women of working age, who suffer from physical disabilities that prevent them at present from earning their own living, can be rehabilitated to the social and economic advantage of Canada, Labour Minister Gregg told the Montreal Klwanis club today.
In conjunction with the provinces and various voluntary agencies, the federal government has in mind giving effect to such a program, he said.
The program, he declared, must include medical treatment, therapy, convalescence, vocational guidance and training. All this will be directed toward eventually placing the rehabilitated person in a suitable job in industry.
That is a field in which much useful work remains to be done and, it seems to me, a very challenging field with which we are confronted in this house, in relation to the problem of making provision for the needs of those who are socially and permanently disabled and without means of support.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I mention just briefly a subject that I have been harping on for many years in this house. In returning to it I feel I need make no apology. I feel there ought to be a select standing committee of this house charged with the responsibility, and I may say, given the opportunity of studying matters pertaining to the health and welfare of this nation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is the minister going to answer some questions now?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I want to thank the hon. members who have taken part in the debate thus far, including the hon. member for Temiscouata who asked me a very important question which I will deal with on the appropriate item, for the level of this debate. I would be lacking in gratitude particularly to the hon. member for Cape Breton South if I did not say at once how much I appreciated his encouraging words about the work we are trying to do in this department.
I do not propose to deal at this hour with all the questions brought up, because I will deal with a lot of them seriatim as we come to the various items.
Supply-Health and Welfare
I shall deal first of all with the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. He referred to the travelling expenses of this department. He referred to them as though they were excessive. I want to say that you cannot run the Department of National Health and Welfare as it should be run without incurring travelling expenses. Remember that our job is one of co-ordination with the provincial departments of health. Our food and drug inspectors carry on a tremendously important job and they are in continuous travel, as they should be. Our officials in the operation of the national health plan, with all of its divisions, are constantly being called upon by the provinces for consultation which involves travel. I am not saying there does not have to be a most careful scrutiny of these expenditures- there has to be-and I assure my hon. friend that there is such scrutiny. What he has failed to point out is that there was actually a decrease in the travelling expenses of the entire department, outside of civil defence.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is that a decrease in the estimate or in comparison with the actual expenditures last year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
In staff. That does not include civil defence, which has been added to this department. That is the statement he should have made instead of letting it go out to the country that this department was profligate. Let my hon. friend show me one instance, instead of making carte blanche remarks which give a wrong impression. I shall take the responsibility as minister for this department. It cannot be run on any other basis. If the hon. member will show me where there has been improper travelling I shall be the first to correct it and I would thank him for it.
Then with regard to information, the hon. member did not point out that our total budget, apart from civil defence, is $72,000 less this year than it was last year. This is not due to the fact that we have cut out important services, but because projected films that had been ordered were not ready for production, for one reason or another. I would say to the hon. member that I would have thought he would be the last man in this house who would criticize this particular aspect of the department's work. He knows, just as the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine pointed out to him, and as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre insisted last year in dealing with this point when replying to the hon. member for Eglin-ton, one of the essential jobs of this department is sending out this kind of information. The department would not be doing its job if it did not make films, and if it did not have
2964	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare pamphlets. I must say that the hon. member was in good form, and I enjoyed his speech. It was just like reading the comic strips which I read every night, and I enjoyed it. It was good fun, but it was not good war.
Every one of the publications to which the hon. member referred, I shall admit, may be a little out of place in the hands of a mature and highly intellectual man like the hon. member. Even I, with my lower intellectual qualities than the hon. member, have had difficulty sometimes in appreciating them. However, there are not many people in the world as mature as he and I, so there have to be ways and means devised of imparting information to those various groups in our population.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There have to be some things to be thankful for.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Seriously, before any publication in our department is approved' by the minister it is first of all gone over with a committee representing the ten provincial departments of health. They aid in distributing the information, and also frequently pass on the form of the material. Apart from the expenditure, they are parties to the projects as I have indicated.
Now then, with reference to the industrial health bulletin to which the hon. member referred, that was one which received the backing of the three large congresses of labour in this country. The hon. member may have his view, but it will be very interesting for those labour organizations to know the view he has taken of the value of this information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The value of your cartoons.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I know what really troubled the hon. member. It was not the value of the information. He and I are old classmates. We have been together many years, and I know him just as well as he knows me. It is just like the old days in college, and Donald does not like to see Paul's name ahead of his. Unfortunately for the hon. gentleman, Mr. Chairman, Paul is the minister, and as long as he is the minister he must accept the responsibility, as he does. If he accepts the responsibility, he has to have his name on the pamphlets, as is the case with every member of any responsible government in this country. If perchance the hon. member should ever become a minister-I do not think there is immediately a great possibility -he will have to subject himself to the inconvenience and embarrassment that attends the use of his name.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: How you hate it!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Lanark made an excellent speech. He was fair


enough to say that many of the things to which he referred were not within the competence of the federal government. As usual he made, I thought, a careful and considered statement. I may tell him that his urging for research, and so on, is something I fully support. This year we are spending $3-5 million on medical research, as compared with less than $1 million five years ago. This covers many fields. It now covers some 112 projects in cancer compared with only two research projects in cancer when the national health program was established. It touches multiple sclerosis, and it touches the various things to which the hon. member made mention. It touches crippling conditions in children, tuberculosis control, cancer control, and mental health.
A few minutes ago one hon. member referred to the need for additional hospitalization in the mental health field. We have assisted in the building of 8,000 additional mental hospital beds. As the hon. member for Lanark pointed out today, together with the provincial governments in a scheme of co-operation we have been able to supply some 38,000 hospital beds in addition to the numbers that existed four years ago. When we come to the various items we can go into further details. Under the national health program the federal government, together with the provinces, has embarked upon a program of the greatest significance to the people of this country. This program has been pursued without political interest, as every provincial department of health will confirm.
I propose to leave most of these subjects for discussion when we come to the various items. I would simply say this. The questions raised by the hon. member for Broadview I think have answered themselves. When he said he was in favour of the existing Swedish system I was most amazed. I think no other person sitting in his group would be in agreement. Certainly, to answer his question directly, I would not give that program my support, nor do I think anyone would who has followed this problem closely.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question at this point? I agree with him. I favour the new plan proposed in Sweden. But just to have the picture clear, has the new plan really been brought into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It was passed by the Swedish legislature, but it has not been brought into effect, although it is a better plan.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No one speaks enthusiastically of it, and I am sure that on reflection and

when he does some research on the matter, the hon. member will agree. I am sure he would not seriously urge that plan in this country. There is nothing further to add.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has spoken with vigour and at length on the matter he raised. In another debate I have stated the present position. All but two of the health surveys are in. The sickness survey, which will be the most significant survey of its kind ever attempted in any country-at least so we are informed by the American medical public association -we hope will be completed soon. We are now making a condensation of the various provincial health surveys which are part and parcel of the nation's health program. I can add nothing more, except to say that I share the view that has been expressed by hon. members who have spoken here tonight as to the importance of this work. There is no department of government that is engaged in more important work, and when we come to these various items the tremendous progress that has been made will be indicated. I have no hesitation in saying at once that there can be no stopping, no letting up in our efforts to try to battle the greatest enemy of mankind, disease. This is something that depends upon the collaboration of governments, the medical profession, the nursing profession, voluntary organizations and so on. I believe that, while we must never relax our efforts, the general picture in this country is one that shows constant activity and continuing interest.

speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question. He made some derogatory remarks about the Swedish plan which I understand is now being revised. That plan has been in existence for many years and has proved satisfactory to a great many people. It just goes to show that anything can be improved; and it would be extraordinary if it could not. If the minister finds so much wrong with the plan which they are changing, he must of necessity have in mind some better plan. I would be greatly interested in hearing what the minister's ideas are on this matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: When we come to that matter we can deal with it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There is no item I know of that deals with health insurance. Will the minister answer that now or under health insurance studies?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes; when we come to the item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Could we not wait until we get to the items?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:

I am asking a question about the details of the first item. At page 318 we find provision for one economist, grade 9; one economist, grade 6; two economists, grade 4; one economist, grade 3; five economists, grade 2; and one economist, grade 1. I note that provision is made this year for what appears to be a doubling of the number of economists in the department.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What specific work are the economists doing; and what work are the additional economists engaged in at the moment?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The national health program is entailing the greatest administrative responsibility and work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are you charging those under this item and not under health insurance studies?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Some of them. They do that as well. We have approved over 3,000 projects. That is a tremendous amount. We have to assess those. Every year we drop some of them; we do not think some should go on. The job of appraising has to be done. These people are assisting in much of that work. That is not their only work. For instance, we have made a study of the various health insurance programs in other countries, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has pointed out, and so on. We really should have more, but that is all I was able to get.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Before I leave that matter, may I get the minister's assurance that when we get to this item he will tell me specifically what he finds fault with in the plan I mentioned?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I shall be glad to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Will he give us the assurance that he will deal with what he told us was a good plan and will he also give us some ideas that he has?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I will not promise to do the latter; but I will tell you what is wrong with yours.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No. I think it only fair that the minister give us some ideas he has after this great length of time he has obviously studied health insurance plans. Will he tel] us what his ideas are and will he tell the committee at that stage when we may expect

Supply-Health and Welfare actually to come to grips with this problem and stop shadow boxing?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext: I am trying to be helpful. At page 319, under the same item, the second last detail, No. 22, we find "Allowances and other expenses of delegates to international conferences, $6,000." May I ask what international conferences the department is sending delegations to this year?

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: There is a question I wanted to ask on item 258. Perhaps while I am on my feet I should say I am glad to note that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has indicated his approval of the new plan suggested in Sweden.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: He said he preferred it to the old one.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I did; but because I prefer my hon. friend to somebody else, that does not mean to say that I prefer my hon. friend to my brother.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: In view of the fact that the minister indicated that the new plan is preferable to the old one, we will point out what the new plan is when we get to the item on health insurance studies. On this item 258, national health branch, I should like to ask the minister what consideration his department is giving to the question we discussed under another heading, namely vitamin E and other drugs in relation to the sales tax and so on. Mr. Chairman, do not get the notion that I am talking about something that should come under the Minister of Finance; because when we discussed this matter with the Minister of Finance he pointed out that his department agrees to the removal of the sales tax on various drugs only when they get a recommendation that this should be done from the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I should be glad if the minister could tell us what progress is being made in his department toward the day when vitamin E will be included among those products so recommended to be free from sales tax. Also what progress is being made in the consideration of other drugs for the same exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I just want to get that item through.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I should like to make even greater progress.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: Just a minute. I know the minister is the Hon. Paul Martin-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I will tell you. The committee is in such a good mood that I ought to be prepared to give a reply to that question. My hon. friend will realize that I cannot very well say in the committee what government policy is until government policy on a particular matter is subscribed to by the government as a whole.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: Or until there is a government policy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: The Minister of Finance, who has great responsibility in these matters, has to take into account the requirements and the money he has available to meet those requirements. I may tell my hon. friend that the department naturally follows these matters with great interest. I cannot say any more than that. I am sure he will understand.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I am sure I would understand that it was the minister speaking even if I could not see him. That is the kind of answer we get far too often. Let us look at the situation. The Minister of Finance says, "We have to consult the Minister of National Health and Welfare". The Minister of National Health and Welfare says, "The Minister of Finance has to consider these matters in the light of his total financial responsibility".

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: Surely the hon. member does not expect me to say that I recommended such and such to the Minister of Finance and that the Minister of Finance did not accept that recommendation. The hon. member surely does not expect me to enter into a discussion of that kind of cabinet debate. I just could not do it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: We understood him to say that he accepted your recommendation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend would recognize the fact that it would be improper for me to enlarge on that any further. I will not say it is improper for him to ask the question, but I doubt if he should persist in it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: Eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I think it is in ordier for us to expect the minister to tell us what the thinking is of the people in his department with regard to vitamin E products and other drugs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: That is a very important matter. My hon. friend can understand the situation. I forgot to say this. For business reasons, even if the situation were otherwise, I could not say in this 'committee what our view is with regard to certain tax relief on certain kinds of drugs.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: If the minister suffers under that disability, some of the rest of us do not. I want to say I feel that vitamin E and a good many other drugs should not be taxed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I was not referring to vitamin E. I was referring to the general problem. There would be companies who would take advantage of what I said, and I do not propose to be put in that position.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I come back again to what I was saying, namely that if we cannot get information out of the minister, at least we can give him information and give him our views.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: I should be glad to have them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES 1951-52
speechtext: There are a great many of us in this chamber who feel it is grossly unfair that these taxes are kept on vitamin E and many other drugs that we might name. Since the Minister of Finance has told us he will not take the tax off unless the Minister of National Health and Welfare recommends that it be done, we urge the Minister of National Health and Welfare to make such a recommendation.
